Ryglice Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Ryglice, Poland

Not demolished. Ryglice, first mentioned in 1301, saw Jewish settlement from the mid-14th century, though written records begin only in 1669; population grew after 1772, when the town joined the Austrian partition and drew resettled Jews from German-held territory. By 1880, Jews made up 14% (372) of residents. Ryglice served as a weaving center; during WWI, at least one Jewish soldier died fighting there and is buried in the local military cemetery. In 1939, 412 Jews lived in town; during WWII, forced laborers were initially buried at their execution site before being exhumed and reburied at this cemetery in 1942. On July 22, 1942, surviving Jews were deported via the Tuchów ghetto to Bełżec. This cemetery was established in the first half of the 19th century; local residents later dismantled its brick fence for construction material. Restoration began in 2004-2006 under the Association for the Restoration of Jewish Heritage in Ryglice, re-erecting tombstones on concrete bases; a 2020 student-led inventory by the AntySchematy2 Foundation identified 175 tombstones and fragments.
